title: Valid Palindrome II
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every single character removal versus resolving only the first mismatch with two pointers.

blocks.text: Given a string s, return true if it can become a palindrome after removing at most one character.

blocks.title: Analogy: One Free Pass to Fix a Broken Mirror Image
blocks.text: Like checking a nearly symmetric pattern that has exactly one flawed spot, and being allowed to remove a single piece to fix the symmetry, if that alone is enough to make it perfectly symmetric.

blocks.caption: At the first mismatch, removing either the left or the right character might fix the palindrome

blocks.text: A mismatch occurs between a and c right away, but removing either one still leaves "bc" or "ab", neither of which is a palindrome, so the answer is false.
It helps to ask exactly which removal positions could ever possibly matter, rather than treating every position as an equally likely candidate.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Valid Palindrome already established the two pointer, converge from both ends, symmetric comparison for checking a palindrome directly, with no removals involved.

Observation 2: Running that exact same scan here, the two pointers keep matching characters correctly until they hit the very first true mismatch, and every character checked before that point on both sides already lines up perfectly.

Observation 3: That first mismatch is the only point in the entire string where a single removal could possibly matter, since removing any character elsewhere leaves the mismatch untouched; at that point, only two candidate fixes exist, skip the left character at the mismatch, or skip the right one, and continue the identical palindrome check on whichever side remains.

Observation 4: Tracing s equal to "abca" confirms it, the pointers match the outer a's, hit a genuine mismatch between b and c, and skipping the left character (b) while continuing the check on the remaining range confirms a valid palindrome, giving the correct answer, true, without ever trying any of the other possible removal positions.
Recognizing that only the very first mismatch offers a meaningful removal candidate is what collapses an O(n) space of possible single-character removals down to exactly two direct checks.
Try removing each character one at a time, and after every single removal, check directly whether the resulting shorter string is a palindrome.

items: For every index i, build a new string with the character at i removed.
Check whether that new string is a palindrome.
If any removal produces a palindrome, return true.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The string is first checked as is, since zero removals is always an acceptable option under "at most one".
Every single index is tried as a removal candidate, rebuilding the string fresh each time and checking it completely independently.
Returning true the moment any removal succeeds avoids checking further positions unnecessarily, but every earlier position must still be tried in the worst case.

blocks.text: Every possible single character removal is directly tried, so if any valid removal exists, it is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), rebuilding and checking a new string for every possible removal.
Space: O(n), for each rebuilt candidate string.

Limitation: most removals do not even need to be considered. Only the very first mismatch found by comparing from both ends actually matters, since only removing the left or right character at that exact mismatch could possibly fix things.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it tries every single removal position, even though a removal far away from any real mismatch obviously cannot fix a broken symmetry.

What running the two pointer scan first fixes: it locates the one and only position where a removal could ever matter, the first genuine mismatch, in a single O(n) pass.

What happens at that mismatch: exactly two candidate fixes exist, skipping the left character or skipping the right one, since one of these two must be the extra character if a valid single removal exists at all.

The core idea: scan until the first mismatch, then check both possible skips directly, with no need to consider any other removal position in the string.

Use two pointers starting from both ends of the string, moving inward as long as characters match. The moment a mismatch is found, only two possibilities remain: either the left character at the mismatch is the one extra character, or the right character is. Check whether skipping the left character (and continuing to compare the rest) produces a full palindrome, or whether skipping the right character does. If either check succeeds, one removal is enough.
Two pointers converge until the first mismatch, then try skipping either side.

blocks.caption: Optimized: at the first mismatch, try skipping either side and check the rest directly

blocks.text: This works because every character pair before the first mismatch already matches symmetrically, so those positions never need to be rechecked; only the region from the mismatch inward, with either the left or right character skipped, needs to be verified, which correctly captures whether the extra character was on the left or the right side of the mismatch.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the initial scan plus at most two additional O(n) palindrome checks after the first mismatch.
Space: O(1), only a few pointers are kept.

blocks.text: The key insight is that only the very first mismatch matters. Once it is found, there are only ever two candidate fixes to check, which turns an O(n) space of possible removals into just two direct checks.

items: Checking every possible single character removal instead of recognizing that only the first mismatch position offers a meaningful candidate fix.
Forgetting to check both the "skip left" and "skip right" options, since only checking one of them can miss a valid answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A string that is already a palindrome, needing zero removals","The two pointer scan detects this by never hitting a mismatch at all."],["A string with more than one character that would need removing","Correctly returns false since only a single removal is allowed."]]}

blocks.text: Emphasize that only the FIRST mismatch matters, not every mismatch, since fixing that one mismatch is a necessary condition for the whole string to become a palindrome with just one removal.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every removal", think: only the first mismatch matters, then try skipping either side.
If the interviewer says "why only two checks after the mismatch", think: the extra character causing the mismatch must be either the current left or the current right character, there is no third option.
If the interviewer says "what if up to two removals were allowed instead of one", think: the same idea generalizes, but now up to two mismatches must each be resolved, and the branching grows accordingly.

items: Why is it sufficient to only examine the very first mismatch, rather than every mismatch in the string?
Why must both the skip-left and skip-right checks be tried, rather than just one of them?
How would this approach change if up to two characters could be removed instead of just one?
How would you also return which character should be removed, not just whether a valid removal exists?
How would you adapt this approach to allow one character to be changed instead of removed?
Valid Palindrome, whose two pointer, converge from both ends, symmetric check is the exact foundation this problem builds one additional branching decision on top of.

Any "almost satisfies a property, fix it with one small change" problem, where identifying the single point of violation first, then trying a small fixed number of local fixes, is the standard technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: two pointers converging from both ends, resolving only the very first mismatch by trying to skip either side.

Core Idea: only the first true mismatch offers a meaningful removal candidate, so checking whether skipping the left or the right character at that single point produces a palindrome is enough, with no need to consider any other position.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a violation at the very first point of mismatch is the only place a single fix could ever matter, collapsing an entire space of candidates down to exactly two.
Interview Difficulty: the two pointer scan itself is standard; remembering to check both skip directions, not just one, is the detail most likely to be missed.
One line memory trick: at the first mismatch, try skipping the left character, then try skipping the right one.
